abstract: Superoxide dismutases (SODs) are key components of the plant antioxidant network, acting alongside catalases, ascorbate peroxidases, peroxiredoxins, and other enzymes to control reactive oxygen species (ROS). Since their discovery in 1969, SODs have been defined by their ability to catalyze the dismutation of superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and molecular oxygen. In this manner, they act upstream of H2O2-scavenging enzymes and connect superoxide removal with downstream peroxide metabolism. Early studies in the 1970s and 1980s established the diversity of SOD isoforms in plants, their subcellular compartmentalization, and their pivotal roles in detoxifying superoxide radicals generated during photosynthesis and respiration. The evolutionary retention of iron SOD, manganese SOD, and copper/zinc SOD in plants reflects the dual endosymbiotic origins of mitochondria and plastids and supports the integration of redox metabolism across cellular compartments. Advances in molecular genetics and biochemistry have revealed SODs to be sensitive markers of plant stress physiology and potential targets for improving crops, although translational efforts in agriculture remain challenging. Beyond their canonical enzymatic functions, recent research highlights the moonlighting roles of SODs in gene regulation, structural assembly, and signaling, positioning them as multifunctional nodes in plant adaptation. This centennial review summarizes the historical milestones, scientific context, and enduring impact of plant SOD research, celebrating its legacy and charting future directions to understand redox biology and crop resilience under intensifying climate pressure.
